questions.prompt: A ServiceAccount is bound to ClusterRole `edit` by a ClusterRoleBinding. To stop it reading Secrets, someone binds it to a new Role that grants only `get configmaps` in its namespace. What can it do afterwards?
choices: Everything edit allows plus get configmaps: RBAC has no deny rules, so permissions are the union of every binding that applies
Nothing, because two bindings for one subject conflict and both are ignored
Only get configmaps, because the narrower Role takes precedence
Everything edit allows except in that namespace, where the Role overrides it
questions.explanation: RBAC is deny-by-default and additive. A request is allowed when any rule of any applicable binding matches; adding a binding can only add permissions. To take Secrets away, change or delete the binding to edit.

questions.prompt: `kubectl auth can-i get pods/log -n shop --as system:serviceaccount:shop:dashboard` prints `yes`, yet the dashboard gets a 403 when it fetches logs. Why?
choices: The answer is cached for ten minutes and the binding was removed
Impersonation does not apply to subresources, so the answer is always yes
Logs are served by the kubelet, which ignores RBAC
kubectl read `pods/log` as a pod named `log`; the log subresource needs `--subresource=log`, and the account's rule covers `pods` but not `pods/log`
questions.explanation: kubectl parses TYPE/NAME, so it asked about get on the pod named log, which a plain `pods` rule allows. The real log request is resource pods, subresource log, which matches only a rule naming `pods/log`, `*/log` or `*`.

questions.prompt: `kubectl auth can-i create selfsubjectaccessreviews -A --as system:serviceaccount:shop:ci` says yes, but a SubjectAccessReview with `spec.user: system:serviceaccount:shop:ci` and no groups says not allowed. Which is right?
choices: kubectl, because SubjectAccessReviews ignore ClusterRoleBindings
Both: impersonation adds the service-account groups and system:authenticated, which the system:basic-user binding grants to, while a SubjectAccessReview evaluates exactly the groups you send
Neither; one of them must be talking to a stale cache
The SubjectAccessReview, because impersonation is not real authorization
questions.explanation: The impersonation filter fills in system:serviceaccounts, system:serviceaccounts:shop and system:authenticated for a service-account user with no --as-group. A SubjectAccessReview takes spec.groups literally. The grant comes from a group binding, so the answers differ for the same user name.

questions.prompt: You create ClusterRole `metrics-reader` with the label `rbac.authorization.k8s.io/aggregate-to-view: "true"`. Who gains its rules?
choices: Nobody until you bind metrics-reader to someone
Only subjects bound to view through a ClusterRoleBinding
Every subject bound to view, and, because view aggregates into edit and edit into admin, every subject bound to edit or admin too
Only service accounts in kube-system, where the aggregation controller runs
questions.explanation: The aggregation controller writes the union of matching ClusterRoles into view's rules. view carries aggregate-to-edit and edit carries aggregate-to-admin, so the rule flows on to both, in every namespace where those roles are bound.

questions.prompt: A CI ServiceAccount may `create rolebindings` in `shop` and holds nothing else. It runs `kubectl create rolebinding self-edit --clusterrole=edit --serviceaccount=shop:ci -n shop`. What happens?
choices: It succeeds, because creating the binding is all it needs
It succeeds, but the binding stays inactive until an admin approves it
Forbidden: it is attempting to grant RBAC permissions not currently held; it would need bind on clusterroles/edit or already hold every permission edit grants in shop
Forbidden, because a RoleBinding cannot reference a ClusterRole
questions.explanation: The RBAC storage checks escalation on every binding create and update: the creator must hold bind on the referenced role or cover all of its rules in that scope. Members of system:masters skip the check. Giving the bot bind on exactly the roles it hands out is the least-privilege fix.

questions.prompt: Which single grant is equivalent to cluster-admin for practical purposes, even though no rule in it says `*`?
choices: `list` on pods in every namespace
`impersonate` on users and groups at cluster scope, because the holder can send any request as any user in system:masters
`get` on configmaps in kube-public
`create` on selfsubjectaccessreviews
questions.explanation: Impersonation makes the API server authorize the request as the impersonated identity. With impersonate on groups, `--as anyone --as-group system:masters` is allowed before RBAC is consulted. bind and escalate are the other two verbs to treat the same way in a review.
